content: The successful treatment of 76,000 individuals with hepatitis C virus (HCV) has been achieved through continuous improvements and simplifications in the HCV testing and treatment pathway. These efforts have addressed key barriers to screening, linkage to care, and treatment, while decentralizing care to primary and non-specialized healthcare sites. In November 2016, a hospital-based screening program was expanded to include rapid antibody testing for all admitted patients. This led to a threefold increase in screening uptake within six months, with monthly screenings rising from 14,623 individuals (May–October 2016) to 46,648 individuals (November 2016–April 2017). In 2018, a pilot project integrating HCV, HIV, and tuberculosis (TB) testing at primary care centers in one region demonstrated a 60% increase in screening coverage. Simplification of diagnostic pathways has been a critical component of the elimination strategy. Following WHO recommendations, rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) or laboratory-based immunoassays are now offered at 1,361 locations nationwide. Initially, patients who tested positive for HCV antibodies had to independently seek viremia testing at specialized clinics, resulting in only 8% of antibody-positive individuals undergoing viral load testing. In 2017, reflex testing was introduced, where antibody-positive specimens are automatically tested for HCV RNA or core antigen, or a new blood sample is drawn immediately after a reactive antibody test. This approach has significantly diversified confirmatory testing, which is now available at over 40 sites using various platforms tailored to different service delivery models. Georgia’s elimination program has evolved toward people-centered healthcare delivery by integrating and decentralizing HCV testing and treatment to primary care and harm reduction sites. By the end of 2019, this model had expanded to 10 locations nationwide, although further expansion was limited by the COVID-19 pandemic. Integration with harm reduction services has significantly increased screening rates among people who inject drugs, from 3,638 tests per year (2006–2014) to 21,551 tests per year after 2015. HCV screening has been integrated with needle and syringe programs (NSPs) at 16 fixed sites and nine mobile units, with some sites offering viremia testing and treatment using GeneXpert technology. Engagement in the care continuum among NSP and opioid agonist maintenance therapy (OAMT) clients has shown high rates of viremia testing (80–86%), treatment initiation (85–87%), and cure (98%). Task sharing has been instrumental in decentralizing HCV care. Initially, only infectious disease specialists could treat HCV, but by early 2016, other specialists, such as gastroenterologists, were authorized to provide care. Primary care physicians were later included, enabling HCV testing and treatment to be integrated into primary healthcare and harm reduction services. In Georgia, Kenya, and Vietnam, peer-based HCV screening and treatment have been integrated into harm reduction services. Peer navigators play a central role in guiding clients through the care cascade, from initial medical assessments to treatment and post-treatment follow-up. This approach has achieved excellent outcomes, with 90% of clients attending all medical appointments and 98% completing treatment. In Vietnam, a collaboration between district-level hospitals and peer-support networks enabled 97% of patients to remain in care during treatment, with a 98% cure rate for those who completed therapy. In Myanmar, where drug use is widespread, Médecins du Monde (MdM) has integrated HCV treatment into its existing HIV-focused harm reduction program. Peer navigators were trained to provide hepatitis awareness sessions, and HCV rapid testing was introduced alongside HIV screening. A GeneXpert instrument was added to one clinic laboratory, and pan-genotypic sofosbuvir/daclatasvir treatment was made available. Despite the challenging humanitarian context, cure rates exceeded 86%, and the program treated the majority of eligible patients within two years. National planning for HCV elimination has been guided by WHO’s 2015 manual, which supports evidence-based decision-making and includes a template for a national hepatitis plan. Simplified algorithms for testing, treatment, and monitoring have been updated to include HCV point-of-care RNA assays, pan-genotypic treatment for individuals aged three years and older, and management of treatment failure. Differentiated care approaches have been adopted to address the specific needs of HCV-infected individuals. Most patients with early-stage liver disease can be treated at the facility or community level, while those with advanced liver disease or complex comorbidities require more intensive clinical support. Integration of HCV services with existing healthcare systems, such as HIV and harm reduction programs, has improved access and efficiency. Combination integrated serological tests for HIV, HBV, and HCV using a single specimen have further enhanced testing efficiency, particularly in high-prevalence populations.
